skill_traces.query:
Andrew: Hey Audrey! Long time no talk! How have you been?
Audrey: Hey! I'm alright. Had some bumps though - last Friday at the park one of my pups saw something and pulled so hard the leash busted. Scared that she might run off and get hurt, so I had to chase after her. Luckily I caught her before anything bad happened. Little moments like this remind me how important she is and how we should be careful when we're out there.
Andrew: Oh man, sorry to hear that! I'm totally getting anxious just thinking about my dog getting lost. Precious must have been really scared. What did you do to calm her down?
Audrey: I petted and hugged her, spoke calmly, and slowly walked her to relax. Our bond feels even stronger when moments like these show up.
Andrew: She looks so adorable! That's the connection I'd like to have with Toby. Any advice on creating a strong relationship with dogs?
Audrey: Building trust with them needs patience and regular training. Give them time and love, and praise their successes.
Andrew: Thanks for the tips! Patience and practice are important for establishing a bond with our pooches, just like any other meaningful relationship. I guess some dogs just need more time! It must be so satisfying to see those successes and progress. Oh, and your pup looks so sharp in that green hat! Is there anything specific you do with them to work on training?
Audrey: Thanks! We work on obedience and teach them tricks like sit, stay, shake, and roll over. It's fun and rewarding for both of us.
Andrew: Wow, teaching them tricks must be super fun! How often do you take them for walks?
Audrey: Very often, multiple times a day even, it's a great exercise for them and great bonding time for us.
Andrew: Hmm that does sound like a great way to bond! What breeds are they again? Their breeds might make a difference regarding how well they bond too.
Audrey: They're all mutts. Two of them are Jack Russell mixes and the other two are Chihuahua mixes. And yea, I believe so! Some dog breeds do bond better than others.
Andrew: Aww, they're all so cute! So much fluff and joy!
Audrey: I love them for that. They really do bring so much joy into my life.
Andrew: Yeah! They really do bring so much into our lives - it's amazing to watch them interact. Here's something I've been taking care of lately. Look at those flowers!
Audrey: Nice! Taking care of something like this relaxes me and brings me peace too. I personally have a small garden as well ya know.
Andrew: That's cool! How's it going?
Audrey: It's going great! The flowers are looking great and my veggie patch is coming along. It's so fun to see them grow! Really feels accomplishing.
Andrew: Those flowers look great! What kind are they?
Audrey: They're called Peruvian Lilies. They are so awesome - they have such bright colors and delicate petals.
Andrew: They're beautiful! So vibrant and eye-catching. Are they difficult to care for?
Audrey: Nope, they're easy to take care of, perfect for me! Just gotta water them and make sure they get enough sun.
Andrew: Awesome! Do they enjoy playing in the garden too?
Audrey: Yeah, they do enjoy the garden! Always running around, exploring and having a great time. So adorable!


Andrew: Wow! Looks like they're having a blast. Are there any other furry pals they play with, or just the ones you have?
Audrey: Just my fur babies.
Andrew: Must be great having them around, the bond between you and them is awesome.
Audrey: Yeah, they do! They make everything so much better. Can't imagine life without them. They mean everything to me.
Andrew: That's such a lovely picture, Audrey! So cute to see them snuggled up, having fun together. They really bring so much joy to our lives.
Audrey: They really do, bringing loads of love and happiness. They are everything to me.

selected.name: Extract Comfort and Joy Sources
selected.description: Use when a message states that something cheers the user up, brings joy, or provides comfort.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a pet, hobby, person, item, or activity that provides cheer, comfort, or emotional support, create a separate durable memory (preference, relationship, or state) capturing that source, even when the message also contains stress or negative events.
Do not merge the supportive source only into a negative-event candidate; it should be its own candidate so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only sources explicitly stated as supportive; do not infer unmentioned ones.
selected.rerank_reason: Audrey explicitly mentions that her dogs bring her joy and comfort, which aligns with the skill's focus on extracting sources of comfort and joy.

selected.description: When a user explicitly states how often they do a recurring activity, extract a durable memory with the activity and frequency.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly states the frequency of a recurring activity (including colloquial phrases like 'very often', 'all the time', 'a couple times a week'), create a candidate memory capturing both the activity and the frequency.
Use memory kind 'state' for habitual routines and 'event' for scheduled recurring occurrences; resolve relative time from the message timestamp.
During CRUD, if a matching memory for the same activity already exists, UPDATE or MERGE it rather than adding a duplicate.
selected.rerank_reason: Audrey states that she takes her dogs for walks 'very often, multiple times a day,' which is an explicit statement about the frequency of an activity.

Use memory kind 'relationship' when the statement defines a connection between the speaker and the subject; otherwise use 'state' or 'preference' for attitudes and values.
Apply to both first mentions and repeated mentions across sessions; record the view as a durable memory rather than folding it into an event memory.
Only extract when the framing is explicit or strongly implied; do not infer relationships from generic pleasantries, compliments, or small talk.
Stop after capturing the explicit view in one memory per stated relationship; do not add redundant memories for every photo or activity that merely implies the same view.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Shared Bonding-Activity Memories
nearby_not_selected.description: When a user reflectively describes a past shared activity with a specific person and frames it as bonding, making memories, or quality time.
content: During extraction, treat first-person statements about a past shared activity with a named person that explicitly mention bonding, making memories, closeness, or quality time as a durable event or relationship memory candidate.
Capture the activity, the companion, and the relational framing.
Do not require explicit fact-like phrasing; reflective storytelling is sufficient evidence.
Create at most one candidate per distinct activity-and-companion pair, and skip statements that name no specific person or activity.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Photo-Sharing Events
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message presents an object or result with visual language like 'Here are...' or explicitly mentions sharing a photo, during extraction.
content: When a message uses presentation phrasing such as 'Here are...', 'Check out...', 'This is a photo of...', or 'Attached is...' to introduce something, record that the speaker shared a photo of that item, even if the word 'photo' does not appear.

If the speaker explicitly mentions sharing, sending, or showing a picture/photo/image, create an event memory that records the sharing action and the described content (e.g., subject or creator of the picture).
Preserve the literal object named in the message (e.g., picture) — do not replace it with an inferred object such as a bookshelf, item, or possession.
Keep the sharing act within the same event memory as the other facts from that message; do not summarize away the visual sharing.
Only include facts explicitly stated; do not convert a shared picture into an ownership claim unless ownership is directly stated.

nearby_not_selected.name: Capture Time Gaps Between Related Events
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message describes an event that references or matches a previously stored event, capture the elapsed time between them as a relationship memory.
content: During extraction, if a message presents an event that explicitly references or parallels a previously stored event (e.g., 'another', 'recently', 'again', 'since last time'), compute the time elapsed between the two events using the message/session timestamps and add one 'relationship' candidate stating that duration.

Also, if the current message describes an event that matches an existing event of the same type for the same subject, compare timestamps or explicit time mentions to compute the elapsed time between the two occurrences and record the temporal relationship.
Only create this candidate when both events are directly evidenced in the session; do not infer unmentioned events or speculate about intervals.
